h.select_rule: Discard any hypothesis whose condition is the edited field's own current value, or whose condition merely disables or disconnects the edited component. From the rest, keep 10 with distinct mechanisms and field pairs, favouring those where an informed expert could plausibly bet on either direction.
h.strategy: Two patterns are banned because experts find them obvious: (1) conditioning on the current value of the same field being edited, which just restates that upgrading a weak setting helps more than upgrading a strong one; (2) conditions that make the edited component unused, unreachable or inert. Instead, each hypothesis must link two DIFFERENT fields that interact through a non-trivial mechanism, such as substitution between parallel routes, a capacity already supplied elsewhere, one part acting as a bottleneck for another, or interference that turns a usually helpful edit harmful. No condition setting may appear in more than two hypotheses. Use the gaps and negated assumptions as the source of each idea. In each 'why', name the mechanism and explain why the opposite direction is also a priori plausible.

hyps.why: A direct identity route already delivers the input to the output, so the marginal gain from a conv on the 0->1->3 route shrinks.
The shortcut substitutes for part of the 0->2->3 path's contribution, reducing the conv's marginal value.
A strong direct conv already supplies spatial capacity, so an upstream conv on the multi-hop route is partly redundant.
A parallel conv route from the input already supplies capacity, making the direct conv more substitutable.
The sibling conv from the input already provides spatial features to nodes 2 and 3, so a second conv into node 1 has diminishing value.
With the direct edge removed, a parameter-free pool on the remaining route costs capacity compared with when the direct edge carries signal.
With edge 0 removed, node 1 is unreachable and the direct edge plus the 0->2->3 route carry everything, so strengthening edge 3 matters more.
Replacing a skip, which is already a strong stabilizing direct route, gives a smaller gain than replacing pool or none.
Swapping an identity for a conv loses the identity's benefit, so the net gain is smaller than when replacing a pool or none.
A parameter-free pool is a weak op to replace, so upgrading it to a conv yields a larger gain than replacing a skip.
